h: Got a letter from BMI, ASCAP, SESAC or GMR?
t: It is real, it is common, and a first letter does not usually go away on its own. Here is what it means and what to do this week. On this page What it isThis weekWhat to avoidHelp

Performing rights organizations (PROs) license the public performance of songs for songwriters and publishers. Bars, restaurants and hotels are among the businesses that take PRO licenses (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015)). ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR each represent their own members’ works, so a venue can need more than one license (SESAC, “What is a performing rights organization?”). A first letter usually offers a license and asks about your venue. Some go on to follow-up contact. In October 2026, music publishers and songwriters affiliated with ASCAP filed copyright infringement lawsuits against hospitality and entertainment businesses in several states, and several complaints reportedly allege repeated licensing contact before suit (Brownstein client alert, “Music licensing under the microscope” (Nov. 9, 2026)). For each work infringed, a court may award statutory damages of $750 to $30,000, up to $150,000 if the infringement is willful, and as little as $200 if the infringer proves it was innocent (17 U.S.C. §504(c), statutory damages). That is the range the law allows, not a prediction for your venue.

- Note the deadline and who sent it. Check that it is a genuine PRO. - List every music use : background music source, live music, DJs, karaoke, TVs, events, social videos. - Gather what you already pay : music service contract and any PRO invoices. - Check your music service terms. Some services state that their license covers the recorded music they supply, and not live bands, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). - Check the small-business exemption if you only play radio or TV broadcasts (see the rules). - Reply on time, with facts. If the letter mentions a lawsuit or comes from a lawyer, talk to a US attorney first.

- Ignoring it. Several lawsuit complaints reportedly describe repeated contact before filing (Brownstein client alert, “Music licensing under the microscope” (Nov. 9, 2026)), so silence tends to prolong the matter rather than end it. - Assuming your music service covers live performances. Services generally cover their own recorded catalog, not live bands, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). - Assuming one PRO license covers everything. Each PRO licenses its own members’ works. - Switching to a personal streaming account. Spotify’s terms grant “personal, non-commercial use” (Spotify End User Agreement, section 3).

h: The venue is responsible, not the performer
t: Each of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs) says the license for performances on your premises is the business’s responsibility: - ASCAP: “the business owner is legally responsible to obtain the license”, and its FAQ adds that live music of any kind, “including DJ nights and karaoke”, needs public performance licenses (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). - BMI: whether music is “performed by a live band, DJ or karaoke, the business owner must obtain permission from the copyright owner” (BMI Music Licensing FAQs). - SESAC: “a business cannot shift its responsibility to musicians or entertainers” (SESAC, who is responsible for paying music licensing fees), and “Paying the band does not cover you” (SESAC FAQ). - GMR: the owner or operator is responsible for the performances on its premises, and paying the performers “will not relieve you of your licensing obligation” (Global Music Rights FAQ). US courts took the same view long ago. h: Your background music service usually stops at background music
t: Business music services license the recorded music they supply for background use. Several say in writing that live entertainment is outside that: - Pandora CloudCover : “A background music license also does not cover live performances, cover artists, DJs”, and the music cannot be integral to the activity, such as karaoke (CloudCover licensing FAQ, updated July 2026). - Soundtrack : If a business “Plays music from another source other than the Service such as a DJ, karaoke, or live music” or “Charges an admission fee”, the public performance rights “are not licensed by Soundtrack” (Soundtrack General Terms, March 2026). - Custom Channels : “Music from DJs, live bands, karaoke, or trivia events is not covered and may require separate PRO licenses” (Custom Channels help center). The PROs describe the same limit from their side. SESAC says a service’s license “only extends to the music they supply to establishments with no admission, membership or similar charge” (SESAC FAQ). ASCAP says karaoke and DJ nights require “additional licensing by the establishment” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs).

h: The DJ’s own subscription is not your license
t: DJs often stream from a DJ service. Some of those services say plainly that the subscription does not cover playing in public: - Beatport: streamed content “is intended for your personal use only”, and public performance “will require additional licensing, which is not included as part of your subscription” (Beatport Streaming terms of use). - VirtualDJ: its Online Music membership “does not give you the right to perform music in public”, and the DJ or the venue needs the public performance licenses (VirtualDJ, Public Performance License). A clause in your booking agreement can say who handles what, but the PRO statements above put the license with the venue.

h: Each PRO licenses only its own songs
t: The four US performing rights organizations (PROs) each say the same thing about their licenses: - BMI: a license from another PRO “allows you only to perform copyrighted music represented by that organization”, because “each PRO licenses a unique repertoire of music” (BMI Music Licensing FAQs). - SESAC: each organization “licenses only the copyrighted works of its own respective copyright holders” (SESAC FAQ). - GMR: licenses with ASCAP, BMI and SESAC “do not grant you authorization” to perform music by GMR’s writers, “and vice versa” (Global Music Rights FAQ). - ASCAP: “you need a license with each PRO that represents the creators of the music that you play” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). So the practical question is not “which PRO is the right one” but “whose songs are played here, and which licenses cover them”. A curated background music service changes the answer for the music it supplies; see Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar?

h: One song can need more than one license
t: Songs are often co-written by writers who belong to different PROs. The U.S. Copyright Office notes that the rights to musical works “are often split among multiple songwriters, with differing publishers and PROs” (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015), p. 123). The Department of Justice describes the result, called fractional licensing: a PRO licenses only its share of a work, “meaning that a licensee must obtain a license from all of the PROs affiliated with the work (or from the songwriters or publishers directly) in order to legally perform it” (DOJ statement closing its review of the ASCAP and BMI consent decrees (January 15, 2021), p. 2).

ASCAP and BMI operate under long-standing antitrust consent decrees with the Department of Justice; SESAC and GMR do not. The Copyright Office puts it this way: “neither SESAC nor GMR is subject to such direct antitrust regulation” (Copyright and the Music Marketplace, p. 34), and the DOJ notes the decrees “regulate only ASCAP and BMI” (DOJ statement, January 15, 2021, p. 2). For a venue, the day-to-day point is simpler: each sets its own fees for bars and restaurants, and each needs its own license. How much does a music license cost? explains what drives those fees.

h: Look up which PRO represents a song

A search tells you who represents a song, not whether your venue is licensed for it. Searching song by song is also impractical for a live band or a DJ, who can play hundreds of titles a night.

h: How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?
t: Each PRO charges separately. ASCAP and BMI base fees mainly on your occupancy and how you use music; SESAC and GMR publish fewer details. On this page What sets the feeASCAP’s 2026 ratesBMI, SESAC and GMRThe totalNext step

The PROs describe broadly similar factors: - How music is used: live, recorded, or audio-visual. ASCAP lists “live, recorded, audio only vs. audio/visual”, the venue’s “capacity”, and “how many nights a week it hosts live music” (ASCAP, why ASCAP licenses bars, restaurants and music venues). - Size. Both ASCAP and BMI tie fees to occupancy; BMI notes occupancy is most commonly set by the local fire marshal (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). - Extras on top of recorded music, such as karaoke and DJs, and any admission or cover charge (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Where you are does not change the ASCAP rate: ASCAP says restaurants of the same size and music use pay the same “regardless of whether the restaurant is in Oshkosh or New York City” (ASCAP).

ASCAP publishes its schedule for restaurants, bars and nightclubs. The annual fee is a rate per occupant, built from the lines below, multiplied by the premises occupancy (if no official occupancy exists, square footage divided by 20). Rates per occupant for calendar year 2026: - Live music, 4 to 7 nights a week : $8.05 - Live music, 3 nights or less : $6.70 - Recorded music, no live music : $4.69 - Recorded music, with live music : $3.10 - Enhancements: karaoke, DJs, emcees, dancing, shows, acts or games : $2.72 - Admission or cover charge : $2.72 - TV or radio only, where the broadcast exemption does not apply : $1.77 The occupancy fee has a minimum of $502, a separate jukebox fee may apply, and the schedule includes adjustments for seasonal venues and an inflation increase each year from 2027. Read the full schedule and its notes before relying on any figure (ASCAP rate schedule and statement of operating policy, calendar year 2026).

- BMI : Says its license “starts at a little more than a dollar per day” and rises with the type of music (recorded, live, DJ, karaoke), how often it is performed, and occupancy (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). - SESAC : Says “music licensing fees vary by industry” and by the degree to which music is used (SESAC, how are fees determined?). - GMR : Says rates “depend upon your type of business and how the music is presented to the public” (Global Music Rights FAQ). We found no published dollar schedule from BMI, SESAC or GMR for bars and restaurants. Ask each for a written quote based on your occupancy and music use.

Because each PRO licenses separately (see Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?), the total depends on how many licenses a venue holds, plus any music service. The National Restaurant Association has said its members pay an average of $4,500 per year to license music (Bloomberg via Indianapolis Business Journal, July 9, 2025). - ASCAP : One of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs). ASCAP says “you need a license with each PRO that represents the creators of the music that you play” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). It publishes a rate schedule for restaurants, bars and nightclubs, with fees per occupant (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- BMI : One of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs). BMI says a license from another PRO “allows you only to perform copyrighted music represented by that organization” (BMI Music Licensing FAQs). For bars and restaurants, BMI says its license “starts at a little more than a dollar per day” and rises with the type of music, how often it is performed, and occupancy (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). - Consent decree : ASCAP and BMI operate under long-standing antitrust consent decrees with the Department of Justice; SESAC and GMR do not. The DOJ notes the decrees “regulate only ASCAP and BMI” (DOJ statement, January 15, 2021, p. 2), and the Copyright Office says “neither SESAC nor GMR is subject to such direct antitrust regulation” (Copyright and the Music Marketplace, p. 34). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR? - Cover charge (Admission charge) : A charge to get in, such as admission or a cover. ASCAP’s 2026 rate schedule adds a line of $2.72 per occupant for an admission or cover charge (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Music services treat it as a limit too: Soundtrack says that if a business “Charges an admission fee”, the public performance rights “are not licensed by Soundtrack” (Soundtrack General Terms), and SESAC says a service’s license “only extends to the music they supply to establishments with no admission, membership or similar charge” (SESAC FAQ). - Direct PRO license : A license a venue takes from a PRO itself, rather than through a music service. - Enhancements : The line in ASCAP’s rate schedule for karaoke, DJs, emcees, dancing, shows, acts or games. For 2026 it adds $2.72 per occupant to the annual rate (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Explained in How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- Fractional licensing (Split works) : Songs are often co-written by writers who belong to different PROs: the rights “are often split among multiple songwriters, with differing publishers and PROs” (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015), p. 123). Under fractional licensing a PRO licenses only its share of a work, “meaning that a licensee must obtain a license from all of the PROs affiliated with the work (or from the songwriters or publishers directly) in order to legally perform it” (DOJ statement, January 15, 2021, p. 2). - GMR (Global Music Rights) : Global Music Rights, one of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs). GMR says licenses with ASCAP, BMI and SESAC “do not grant you authorization” to perform music by its writers, “and vice versa”, and that its rates “depend upon your type of business and how the music is presented to the public” (Global Music Rights FAQ). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- Live performance (Live music, DJs and karaoke) : Music performed on the premises by a band, a DJ or karaoke. Each of the four PROs says the license for performances on a venue’s premises is the business’s responsibility, not the performer’s (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, GMR). SESAC puts it as “Paying the band does not cover you” (SESAC FAQ). Business music services generally do not cover live performances (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). Explained in Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke?

- Occupancy : The capacity figure that ASCAP and BMI use to set their fees. BMI notes occupancy is most commonly set by the local fire marshal (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). In ASCAP’s 2026 schedule, the annual fee is a rate per occupant multiplied by the premises occupancy; if no official occupancy exists, square footage divided by 20 (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). - Performing rights organization (PRO) : An organization that licenses the public performance of songs for songwriters and publishers. SESAC and GMR publish their own searches (SESAC repertory search, Global Music Rights search). A search tells you who represents a song, not whether your venue is licensed for it. Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?

- SESAC : One of the four US performing rights organizations (PROs). SESAC says each organization “licenses only the copyrighted works of its own respective copyright holders” (SESAC FAQ), and that “music licensing fees vary by industry” and by the degree to which music is used (SESAC, how are fees determined?). h: What happens if a restaurant or bar plays music without a license?
t: Usually letters and calls come first, and sometimes a federal lawsuit follows. Here is what the PROs and the statute say, step by step. On this page How it unfoldsWhat the law allowsWho may be liableWhat to do

US copyright law gives the owner of a song the exclusive right “to perform the copyrighted work publicly” (17 U.S.C. §106(4)). Performing rights organizations (PROs) such as ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR license that right to businesses on behalf of songwriters and publishers. The PROs’ own descriptions point to a gradual path: - Letters and calls. ASCAP says that when a bar or club owner refuses a license, it will sue, “but this only happens after many attempts to educate them about their obligations under Federal law” (ASCAP, why ASCAP licenses bars, restaurants and music venues). A BMI spokesperson told Bloomberg that lawsuits are “always a last resort” and that BMI “spends sometimes years on educational outreach” (Bloomberg via Indianapolis Business Journal, July 9, 2025). - A visit. In the same report, BMI said that if those efforts are ignored, “an in-person visit might occur, and BMI may take legal action” (Bloomberg via IBJ). - A lawsuit in federal court. Copyright cases are heard by federal district courts: “No State court shall have jurisdiction” over them (28 U.S.C. §1338(a)). On March 10, 2026, ASCAP announced “11 separate copyright infringement actions against establishmen

Federal copyright law sets out what a court may order when it finds infringement. The quotes below come from the statute itself. - Damages, two ways : An infringer is liable for either the copyright owner’s “actual damages and any additional profits of the infringer”, or statutory damages (17 U.S.C. §504(a)). h: Holiday songs are licensed like any other music
t: US copyright law gives the owner of a musical work the exclusive right “to perform the copyrighted work publicly” (17 U.S.C. §106(4)). A work is performed “publicly” when it is performed “at a place open to the public or at any place where a substantial number of persons outside of a normal circle of a family and its social acquaintances is gathered” (17 U.S.C. §101, definitions). Neither section treats seasonal music differently from music played the rest of the year. Many of the best-known holiday songs are recent enough to be under copyright. ASCAP’s 2025 chart of its 25 most-played holiday songs, “all written, co-written or arranged by ASCAP songwriters and composers”, includes “Sleigh Ride” (1948), “Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer” (1949), “White Christmas” (1941) and “All I Want for Christmas Is You” (1994) (ASCAP’s 2025 holiday charts, as reported by BroadwayWorld, December 11, 2025). All of them were written after the public-domain cutoff explained below. Each performing rights organization (PRO) licenses only its own catalog; Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR? explains how the four fit together.

h: Old carols: the song, the arrangement and the recording
t: Copyright in older works does run out. The U.S. Copyright Office states that “all works published in the United States before January 1, 1931, are in the public domain” (U.S. Copyright Office, Circular 15A, revised April 2026). Works published in 1930 entered the US public domain on January 1, 2026 (Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain, Public Domain Day 2026). The Office also cautions that “there are a number of exceptions” to its general guidance: “In many cases, it is important to consult with a copyright attorney before reaching any conclusions regarding the copyright status of a work” (U.S. Copyright Office, Circular 22, How to Investigate the Copyright Status of a Work, revised April 2026). What a venue plays is rarely the bare carol. It is a particular arrangement in a particular recording, and each layer is looked at separately: - The song : The words and music as first published. If they were published in the US before 1931, the general rule above applies to them. - The arrangement : The Copyright Act lists a “musical arrangement” as a derivative work (17 U.S.C. §101). h: Step 1: List the music uses you plan
t: Start with a plain list of every way music will be heard in the venue, room by room. The license follows the business: ASCAP says “the business owner is legally responsible to obtain the license” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). Each use below has its own answer page. - Background music : The playlist in the dining room, bar, patio and restrooms. Where it comes from matters; see step 2 and Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar? - Live music, DJs and karaoke : ASCAP says live music of any kind, “including DJ nights and karaoke”, needs public performance licenses (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). More in Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke? - TVs and radio : A narrow exemption can cover certain radio and TV broadcasts in smaller venues, within equipment limits. It never covers streaming services, live music or music in social videos. See Is my venue exempt from music licensing? - Private events and special nights : A band or DJ booked for a party, a ticketed night or a cover charge is a live use like any other. GMR says paying the performers “will not relieve you of your licensing obligation” (Global Music Rights FAQ). - Social video : Music added to an Instagram, TikTok

h: Step 2: Choose your background music source
t: Consumer streaming plans are written for personal listening. Spotify, for example, grants permission for “personal, non-commercial use” (Spotify End User Agreement, section 3) Playing a personal plan to customers goes beyond those terms. A business music service is the usual alternative. It generally covers its own recorded catalog played as background music, and not more: Pandora CloudCover says “A background music license also does not cover live performances, cover artists, DJs” (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). Read your service’s terms for what it includes, and keep a copy. The options are compared in Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar?

h: Step 3: Contact each PRO whose catalog you will play
t: There are four US performing rights organizations (PROs), and each licenses only its own catalog. ASCAP: “you need a license with each PRO that represents the creators of the music that you play” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). GMR says licenses with the other three “do not grant you authorization” to perform its writers’ music, “and vice versa” (Global Music Rights FAQ). Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR? explains how the four fit together and how to look up a song. Each PRO has its own starting point for businesses. Described as the PROs’ own pages showed them on November 13, 2026: - ASCAP : ASCAP’s page for music users lists a “Restaurant, Bar & Nightclub Music License” with a “Purchase License” button. For other businesses it says: “Can’t find your business type? Fill out our licensing contact form and one of our representatives will be in touch with you with the music license that fits your needs” (ASCAP, music licensing for businesses). - BMI : BMI’s FAQ says that whether music is “performed by a live band, DJ or karaoke, the business owner must obtain permission from the copyright owner”, and that a license from another PRO “allows you only to perform copyrighted music repre

h: Step 4: Keep records, and recheck when things change
t: Keep one folder with each license agreement and invoice, your music service contract and terms, and the step 1 list of music uses. It makes renewals simpler and gives you something clear to compare against any letter you receive later. Got a letter from a PRO? covers what to do if one arrives. Look at the list again whenever the music changes: a first live night, a DJ or karaoke night, a cover charge, private events, more TVs or speakers, or a new music service. A background music service usually stops at background music (step 2), and GMR says its rates “depend upon your type of business and how the music is presented to the public” (Global Music Rights FAQ). A change in how you use music can mean a change in what you need. For a printable version of these questions, see the music licensing checklist.
